item.title: Calligraphy in Kyoto: A Shodo Brush Experience — Guide
item.description: Shodo, the way of writing, is one of Japan’s most revered arts, and a calligraphy experience in Kyoto is a quiet, meditative counterpoint to sightseeing. Guided by a teacher in a studio, machiya or temple, you begin by grinding an ink stick against a stone with water — a slow ritual that settles the mind — before learning to hold the brush and form the strokes of a character in the correct order and rhythm.

item.title: Osaka Okonomiyaki Cooking Class: Grill Your Own — Guide
item.description: Okonomiyaki, the hearty savoury pancake of cabbage, batter and toppings grilled on a hot iron plate, is Osaka’s defining home-style dish, and a cooking class is one of the most enjoyable ways to get under the skin of the city’s food culture. In a small group around a teppan, an instructor walks you through mixing the batter, grilling and the all-important flip, then eating what you’ve made hot off the plate, usually finished with sauce, mayonnaise, bonito flakes and seaweed.

item.title: Wagashi Making Class in Kyoto: Shape Your Own Sweets — Guide
item.description: A wagashi-making class is one of the most rewarding hands-on experiences in Kyoto, a direct way into the city’s refined sweet-making tradition. Under the guidance of a confectioner, you learn to shape nerikiri — a smooth, pliable dough of sweet white-bean paste — by hand and with simple tools into the seasonal flowers, leaves and motifs that define kyo-wagashi. It is finer and more meditative work than it looks, demanding a gentle touch, and at the end you sit and eat the two or three sweets you have made with a bowl of matcha.

item.title: Zen Meditation in Kyoto: A Zazen Experience — Guide
item.description: As the historic centre of Rinzai Zen, Kyoto is the best place in Japan to try zazen, the seated meditation at the heart of Zen practice. A number of temples run sessions open to visitors, some in English, in which a monk guides you in the posture, breathing and stillness of zazen in a quiet hall, often followed by a short dharma talk and a bowl of tea. In the traditional style, an attendant may walk the hall with the keisaku, a flat wooden stick used to strike the shoulders — not as punishment but, on request, to restore focus.

item.title: Nada Sake Blending Workshop: Make Your Own Bottle — Guide
item.description: Blending — deciding how different tanks are combined into the final product — is one of the quiet arts of sake brewing, and a few Nada breweries now let visitors try it. You are given a set of base sakes that differ in rice variety, yeast, polishing ratio and age, a measuring cylinder and a tasting glass, and talked through how each component behaves: one contributing aroma, another body, another acidity or a dry finish.

item.title: Okinawa Karate Guide: The Birthplace, Dojos & Experiences
item.description: Okinawa is the birthplace of karate, which grew from the indigenous Ryukyu fighting art “te” blended with Chinese martial influences. For practitioners worldwide, training in Okinawa is a pilgrimage to the source; for travellers, it’s a rare chance to step into a traditional dojo and learn the basics — stances, blocks, strikes and the spirit of respect at the heart of the art. With beginner-friendly experiences and the impressive Okinawa Karate Kaikan, anyone can connect with this living heritage.

item.title: Osaka Kendo Class Guide: Try the Way of the Sword
item.description: Behind the thunderous shouts and clashing bamboo of a dojo lies kendo — “the way of the sword,” the modern martial art descended from samurai swordsmanship. A kendo experience class in Osaka lets visitors step onto the dojo floor, grip the bamboo shinai, learn a few basic cuts and stances, and even try on a piece of the armour, all under an instructor who explains the discipline, spirit, and etiquette behind it.

item.title: Osaka Takoyaki Cooking Class Guide: Flip Your Own Octopus Balls
item.description: Eating takoyaki in Osaka is essential — but making it is a different kind of fun. The mesmerising flick-and-turn that shapes runny batter into perfect crisp spheres is genuinely tricky, and a takoyaki-making class lets you try it yourself on a real dimpled pan, with a local teacher guiding your wrist. It’s hands-on, hilarious, and you eat your wonky-but-delicious results at the end — one of Osaka’s most enjoyable and very on-brand experiences for foodies, couples, and families.

item.title: Tokyo Ramen Cooking Class Guide: Make Your Own Bowl from Scratch
item.description: You can eat extraordinary ramen all over Tokyo — but learning to make it transforms how you understand Japan’s most beloved comfort food. A ramen cooking class takes you behind the steaming counter: building a broth, understanding the four components that define every bowl, hand-preparing the toppings, and finally assembling — and eating — a bowl of ramen you made yourself. It’s hands-on, delicious, conducted in English, and one of the most rewarding food experiences in the city, especially for travellers who want to take a real skill home.

item.title: Tokyo Sushi Making Class Guide: Learn from a Trained Itamae
item.description: Sushi looks deceptively simple — a slice of fish on a mound of rice — but every element conceals years of craft. In a Tokyo sushi-making class, a trained itamae (sushi chef) reveals those secrets: how to season and handle the rice, how to wield a Japanese knife, and how to shape nigiri and roll maki with the right pressure and form. You leave not only having eaten beautiful sushi you made yourself, but with knife and rice fundamentals that quietly change how you eat — and make — sushi for the rest of your life.

item.title: Hiroshima Mystery & Escape Rooms: Real-Life Puzzle Adventures
item.description: Japan invented the modern “real-life escape game” — known here as Real Escape Game (リアル脱出ゲーム) — and the format has matured into a national pastime with dozens of operators producing increasingly elaborate puzzle experiences. Hiroshima’s scene is smaller than Tokyo’s or Osaka’s but offers a satisfying mix of permanent escape room venues, walking mystery tours, and history-themed puzzle experiences specific to the prefecture. This guide covers what’s actually available for overseas visitors, including English-friendly options.
